title: Arrays of strings and arrays of character pointers
learningObjectives: Declare arrays of character arrays for fixed-capacity writable strings.
Declare arrays of char pointers and understand that they store addresses.
Explain the lifetime and mutability differences between string literals and writable arrays.
Use const char pointers when referring to read-only string literals.
Choose a representation based on ownership, capacity and whether each string must be modified.

understand.concept: An array of character arrays stores multiple strings in separate fixed-size rows, while an array of char pointers stores pointer values that refer to character sequences elsewhere. The rows in a character matrix provide writable storage for each string, whereas pointers may refer to string literals or other objects with different lifetimes and mutability. These representations have different memory layouts and ownership requirements.
understand.whyItMatters: This knowledge helps reason about C data representation, object bounds and valid memory access.
understand.analogy: Think of memory objects as labelled storage and pointers as typed references to that storage.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal pointer, lifetime and object-access rules.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Array of character arrays

`char names[3][12]` reserves three rows, each with capacity for up to eleven non-null characters plus a terminator. Each row is writable and has storage within the containing array.

## 2. Array of pointers

`const char *names[] = { "Ada", "Grace", "Linus" };` creates an array of pointers. Each pointer refers to a string literal. The pointer elements can be changed, but the pointed-to literal must not be modified.

## 3. Storage and lifetime

A character matrix stores the character bytes inside the matrix object. An array of pointers stores addresses; the pointed-to data may live elsewhere. Ensure every pointer remains valid for as long as it is used.

## 4. Mutability

Use `char names[][12]` when each row needs writable character storage. Use `const char *` when referring to read-only text. Do not discard const qualification and then attempt to modify a string literal.

## 5. Select intentionally

A matrix has a fixed row capacity and may waste space when strings vary greatly in length. A pointer array is flexible but requires clear ownership, lifetime and capacity rules for every pointed-to string.

examples.title: Writable array of strings
examples.explanation: Each row has its own fixed writable storage and room for a terminator.

examples.title: Array of pointers to read-only literals
examples.explanation: The array stores three pointer values. Each points to a string literal that should be treated as read-only.

practise.guidedTask: Implement a small C program demonstrating CL4.9. Identify the relevant array or string capacity, valid indices, expected results and failure cases before compiling and testing.
practise.independentTask: Create a second example for CL4.9 that handles a boundary case explicitly. Add tests for empty input, the smallest valid case, the largest valid case and one invalid or oversized case. Explain how your code prevents invalid access.

options: Three rows, each with 12 char elements
questions.answer: Three rows, each with 12 char elements
questions.explanation: It is an array of three arrays, each containing twelve char elements.

questions.prompt: What does an array of char pointers store?
options: Pointer values that refer to character sequences
All string bytes inline in one fixed matrix
questions.answer: Pointer values that refer to character sequences
questions.explanation: Each array element is a pointer.

questions.prompt: Why use const char * for string literals?
options: To express that the pointed-to literal must not be modified
To make the pointer itself impossible to change
To allocate a writable copy automatically
questions.answer: To express that the pointed-to literal must not be modified
questions.explanation: The pointed-to data is read-only through this pointer type.

questions.prompt: Which representation provides writable fixed-capacity rows?
options: An array of pointers to string literals
questions.explanation: Each row is part of the array object and can be modified.

questions.prompt: What must be considered when using an array of pointers?
options: The lifetime, validity and mutability of each pointed-to string
Only the number of pointer variables
questions.answer: The lifetime, validity and mutability of each pointed-to string
questions.explanation: The pointers do not own or guarantee the lifetime of their target data.
